stories.body:
Introduction: Global stocks tumble as AI panic grips markets

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Fears that the Democratic Party’s blue wave in this week’s midterm elections will sink the AI investment boom are roiling markets, following heavy losses on Wall Street last night.

Asia-Pacific markets are a sea of red (unlike the US election map on Tuesday night!), as investors ditch tech stocks after more than $3.2tn was wiped off the US stock market yesterday.

Today, Japan’s Nikkei stock index has slumped by almost 6% – its worst drop since April 7 2025 during the ‘liberation day’ tariff panic.

South Korea’s KOSPI is down 6.7%, and Taiwan’s TAIEX has dropped by 4.5% in a broad rout.

Christopher Forbes , head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets , called the market action “a bit of a disaster”, explaining ( via Reuters ):

double quotation mark “(Clients) were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. “All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints, ... because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money. “And it’s not just a slap in terms of valuation. It’s basically a whole policy and six-year structural shift that says we’re now going to pause, we’re now going to cool AI, we’re now going to cool data centres, approvals and equity capital markets.”

After months of warnings that AI valuations were too high, and that the bubble might burst, US investors dashed to the exits en masse yesterday. The Nasdaq tech index slumped by 5.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and the S&P 500 lost 4.36%.

Memory chip makers, who had been profiting from the AI boom, led the fallers – SanDisk slumped 22% and both Micron and AMD lost 17% of their value.

Chip giant Nvidia led the fallers on the DJIA , down over 9%.

Analysts pointed to policy uncertainty as Democrats are more critical of data centres, which could slow the rollout of AI investment – especially given public opposition to the sector .

Kyle Rodda , senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, says it was a “brutal sell-off” as fears about the future of the AI buildout gripped the markets.

double quotation mark The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom. The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations. Earnings season has been an overall disappointment for the markets, with Magnificent Seven results so far undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down.

So, it could be a ‘tin hats on’ day in the markets. Investors will also be watching the latest US jobs report, for clues into the health of America’s labour market.

The agenda

7am GMT: Lloyds house price index

9am GMT: UN’s FAO food price index

1.30pm GMT: US non-farm payrolls jobs report

3pm GMT: University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence report

The UK’s smaller share index, the FTSE 250, is also having a bad day.

The FTSE 250 is down 1.25% today, just a day after hitting an alltime intraday record high.

The index contains more domestic companies than the FTSE 100 , so is a better gauge of the health of the UK economy.

US inflation data due next Tuesday could determie whether the sell-off continues, or not, predicts Daniela Hathorn , senior market analyst at Capital.com :

double quotation mark Global markets are ending a turbulent week in which the US midterm elections, concerns about AI investment and renewed uncertainty around interest rates have triggered significant volatility. What initially looked like a technology-led correction has developed into a broader reassessment of risk, with Thursday’s sharp selloff on Wall Street highlighting how quickly concerns about one sector can spread across financial markets. Looking ahead, next week’s US inflation figures could prove decisive in determining whether equities stabilise or face another round of selling.

That inflation report will show how much pressure is building on the US Federal Reserve to hike interest rates to quash inflation….

The UK’s FTSE 100 share index is heading for its worst day since March despite not containing many tech stocks.

Some of the largest fallers, such as advertising group WPP (-4.9%) and data analysis form Relx (-4.44%), are companies who are thought to be under threat from AI , showing it is a broader sell-off.

Musk's wealth has fallen by $113bn since midterms

The post-midterms market rout has been particularly painful for Elon Musk.

Musk (who put $446m of support into Republican campaigns), has lost around $113bn of wealth in the last two days.

This is because his two largest companies have both been badly hit in the sell-off.

Tesla fell 3.34% on Wednesday, as investors reacted to the Democrats’ electoral success, then 10.7% on Thursday. Musk owns 17.7% of the carmaker.

SpaceX lost 3.8% on Wednesday, then 9% yesterday – which also hurt Musk as he owns 10.3% of it.

In total, Musk’s paper wealth fell by $33.5bn on Wednesday, and then by another $79.7bn yesterday, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index .

Despite this, Musk is still the world’s richest person with a paper wealth of $785bn, more than double Jeff Bezos in second place with $370bn.

Stock markets in developing nations have hit their lowest level in seven months today.

The MSCI Emerging Markets Index is down 2.7%, touching its lowest level since April and heading for a sixth straight weekly decline, Reuters reports .

London market on track for worst day since March

The sell-off in London is gathering pace!

The FTSE 100 share index is now down 189 points, or 1.75%, to 10,593 points.

That would be its biggest one-day drop since 19 March, when the Iran war was hitting the markets.

The US dollar is strengthening today, often a sign that investors are seeking safe-haven assets.

That’s pushed the pound down by over half a cent to $1.3387.

This had been a bumper week for the pound – it hit its highest level since the Brexit vote against a basket of currencies.

Yesterday’s slump in the Nasdaq suggests we have just seen “mass capitulation”, argues Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell , explaining:

double quotation mark [Investors have] sold tech indiscriminately, most likely to lock in any profits they’ve made in recent years given the sector’s previous superior wealth generating capabilities. “Others might have had no choice but to sell if they’ve borrowed to buy shares. Margin calls can require leveraged investors to put up more cash or sell some of their holdings, with that forced selling adding to downward pressure on the market ( as flagged earlier ).

Photos: Markets fall

There were concerned faces on the floor of the New York stock exchange yesterday, as the market suffered its biggest one-day drop in about 19 months:

This fed though to Tokyo, where pedestrians were shown the damage on the Nikkei stock exchange, which fell 6%:

Dealers were busy at Hana Bank in Seoul, South Korea, where the Kospi share index lost 6.5%.

BlueBay: AI slowdown might help the hyperscalers

The companies rolling out AI data centres might actually benefit, in the long term, if politicians throw some sand into the wheels of the industry.

That’s because the planned pace of AI rollout has been so quick that it’s forced these hyperscalers (such as Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Google) into hectic sales of debt and shares to fund new multi-billion dollar supply deals.

Mark Dowding of RBC BlueBay Asset Management explains that this could actually make hyperscalers a more attractive investment, saying:

double quotation mark Indeed, a regulatory-induced slowing of AI-related projects may actually help ensure that the pace of growth is more sustainable going forward. Over recent months, constant upward revisions in spending plans have led to a deluge of debt and equity issuance, which has been weighing heavily on markets, with demand failing to keep pace with supply. Should this now slow somewhat, RBC BlueBay think that spreads for hyperscalers may stabilise. Consequently, the firm consider adding exposure in that space, having previously been very sceptical of the prospects for AI-related debt over the course of the past year.

Wall Street futures show Nasdaq may rise

Just in: Wall Street appears to be on track for a calmer day than yesterday!

Technology shares are expected to rise a little after Thursday’s slump.

That’s based on the latest futures market data, which gives an indication of how shares might move when trading begins in New York at 9.30am EST (or 2.30pm UK time).

They show that S&P 500 e-mini futures are up 0.2%, Nasdaq 100 future are up 1.1%, but Dow Jones industrial average futures are down 0.8%

Some context: The S&P 500 is a broad measure of the US stock market, tracking companies in sectors from financials and healthcare to technology, industrials and energy.

The Dow is much narrower – just 30 large US companies.

And the Nasdaq 100 is the one hundred largest tech stocks on Wall Street (eg Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, Alphabet, Tesla…)

But there’s still more than five hours until Wall Street opens, so we shall see!

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, warns there is a risk of further losses.

double quotation mark “Yesterday’s brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come. Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, likely to drive a risk-off move across a broader swathe of equities, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”

Reuters: Tech selloff wipes out hedge fund gains, leads to layoffs

Technology stocks have been dropping since early October, when the Nasdaq Composite hit a record high.

Those losses have been painful for hedge funds who had used borrowed money to back tech stocks (using ‘leverage’, in market jargon).

As the markets have fallen, those leverage bets will have turned sour, prompting margin calls (when your broker demands more cash or collatoral to cover a losing position).

Reuters reports:

double quotation mark Several large multi-manager hedge fund platforms have cut leverage and laid off loss-making teams in recent weeks, said market participants, who expect more layoffs if declines continue. The post-US midterm market turmoil extended losses after a bruising October, when sentiment was dampened by elevated AI-related borrowing costs and worries over returns. The Nasdaq 100 index, which contains many tech heavyweights, plunged 6.6% last month, its biggest monthly fall in 18 months. JPMorgan estimates global hedge funds lost 3% in October.

Jefferies: don't see Democrats giving up on AI growth engine

Interestingly, Jefferies economist Mohit Kumar doesn’t believe yesterday’s losses are “the start of the unwind of the AI trade”.

Kumar argues:

double quotation mark We do admit that policy uncertainty after the Blue Tsunami raises concerns over AI investment and the pace of data center buildup. However, data centers and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move onto other states or outside the country. AI investment has been a key driver of US growth, and we do not see Democrats as giving up on this growth engine.

Market sell-off: what the experts say

There was a huge slump in the most AI-exposed parts of the US stock market yesterday, Jim Reid of Deutche Bank told clients this morning:

double quotation mark In fact, the scale of the moves ranked among the biggest in years, and the Philly semiconductor index (-12.25%) had its worst day since the pandemic slump in March 2020 . And in turn, that cascaded elsewhere, with the S&P 500 (-4.36%) posting its biggest slump since the Liberation Day volatility in April 2025 . So that drove a huge surge in the VIX index (+11.6pts), which also saw its biggest daily jump since the Liberation Day period, ending the session at 28.2pts, its highest since March.

Mohit Kumar, economist at investent bank Jefferies , doesn’t expect a quick rebound from yesterday’s losses.

He writes:

double quotation mark In previous episodes of retail selling, institutional investors have stepped in to find value. The approaching year-end complicates the behaviour of institutional accounts as risk appetite would be limited…. The geopolitical uncertainty around possible US action in Iran also suggests that investors would not rush to add risk.

Stuart Clark , portfolio manager at Quilter , points out that the dominance of the tech sector exacerbated yesterday’s selloff:

double quotation mark “The blue wave at the ballot box has quickly been replaced by a sea of red on investors’ screens. Technology stocks have sold off sharply, with the immediate catalyst appearing to be concerns around tougher AI regulation, covering both the models themselves and the vast data centre infrastructure required to support them. “The scale of the falls in some of the market’s biggest names has been striking. But it also highlights the concentration risk that has built up in US equity markets. With a relatively small number of technology and semiconductor stocks now carrying so much weight, weakness in those names quickly translates into sizeable falls for the Nasdaq and S&P 500.

Ahead of this week’s losses, there were plenty of warning signs that markets might have risen too fast.

As my colleague Richard Partington and I wrote in late September, the warning lights were “flashing red” as the fighting in the Middle East intensified, a slowdown loomed in the AI arms race, and government borrowing costs hit multi-decade highs.

One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – had risen to its highest level since 2000 by September, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits.

This week’s losses have pulled the CAPE ratio down ( you can see it here ), but it’s still historically high:

Reasons not to panic

Amid the scary-everything-is-bad-in-stocks news, it’s easy to feel a bit worried about pensions or savings, my colleague Siraj Datoo writes.

And yes, yesterday was a bad day in particular for technology stocks, with the Nasdaq losing $2.5tn in market capital in a single day.

But it’s worth taking a second to pause. While many of the charts leading newspaper homepages are fairly narrow, showing the dramatic fall in just a few days, if you look at the Nasdaq, the US index mostly dominated by tech stocks, from the start of the year, it’s still up 4.6% YTD ( see previous post for more details ).

Of course, this correction still could have room to run and markets are famously emotional. But there have been warnings about this. Michael Burry, the famous fund manager behind The Big Short, has been screaming from the sidelines about overvaluations in the tech world.

One of the major concerns right now is the huge data centre buildout in the US and whether Democrats will place restrictions or slow things down. That’s a problem for investors because so many of the world’s biggest companies have invested enormous amounts of money -- often taking on additional debt -- to fund their deep investment. The bet is that the artificial buildout will eventually generate big returns but investors are now increasingly worried about just how long that will take.

stories.body:
Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget

Published 5 November 2026

The Northern Ireland secretary has said that it is not his "job" to set a budget and that it is the responsibility of the Northern Ireland Executive.

This comes after no resolution was reached in negotiations between executive parties and Sir Chris Bryant.

He is understood to have presented a set of conditions, including revenue raising, to be attached to any potential deal on a Stormont budget.

Sir Chris said: "They really have to take me seriously when I say there is no more money."

Seven months into this financial year the Northern Ireland Executive has still not agreed a budget.

Speaking after a series of one-to-one meetings, the First Minister Michelle O'Neill said there was still "no white smoke".

Democratic Unionist Party leader (DUP) Gavin Robinson said he felt there was a level of optimism that was "not matched by the reality inside" the room during talks.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant (right) greets Finance Minister John O'Dowd at Hillsborough Castle

Speaking on BBC Newsline , Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget.

He described talks ending without agreement as "a bit frustrating" but added that he's still "hopeful".

He said: "I just wanted to get a move on" and added: "Whatever the total envelope is you have to live within it".

Sir Chris also said he would only set a budget for Northern Ireland if the executive parties asked him to.

"They should be able to put together their budget but they have to decide what their priorities are."

The Sinn Féin delegation was made up of Michelle O'Neill, John O'Dowd, Mary Lou McDonald and Caoimhe Archibald

After talks with the secretary of state, the first minister said that while there may be things dividing the executive, her party would persist in trying to get a budget deal done that allows public sector pay awards to be made for this year.

O'Neill also said she was getting "impatient" with the government and that she would take no lectures from it about managing finances.

Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson said the secretary of state is "not moving"

The DUP leader said: "As it stands today, the secretary of state is not moving, the practical, honest reality of that is that without additional resource, there will not be a balanced budget".

Robinson added that "there will be no legal ability to do what it is we think the executive needs to do, and what we want it to do" without a budget.

Bryant says executive should improve 'discipline'

Stormont ministers argue the UK's devolution funding formula no longer delivers enough for them to balance their books.

The government had offered them an additional £525m this year, but they said it still left significant gaps in managing their spending pressures, particularly delivery of pay awards for public sector workers.

It is not clear what the shape of a final budget agreement could look like, with some parties insisting there is still scope to "reprofile" some of the financial package.

Bryant's conditions are believed to include the executive committing to £200m in additional revenue raising in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

He has also asked that they should improve "discipline" around promises and delivery of pay parity to public sector workers in Northern Ireland.

Health Minister Robbie Butler, UUP leader Jon Burrows and Steve Aiken spoke to the media outside Hillsborough

Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows said he did not want to sound "defeatist" and would continue to engage with the government.

But he said there was a real prospect that it would be resolved in time to avert the potential of strike action by health care workers waiting on pay uplifts for this year.

Speaking before talks with the secretary of state, Alliance's Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir said it is now "make your mind up time" for the executive.

"This needs to be resolved not in weeks or months, but days. We need to come to a final conclusion and give certainty to people who deserve proper pay but also in terms of investment in public services we need to get this done," he added.

Speaking on BBC NI's The View programme, Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna said a budget is "an agreement to take responsibility and an agreement to prioritise".

Her party, which is the official opposition in the legislative assembly, is "very clear about the severe constraints," she said, but added: "the fact is by not having a budget in month eight of this financial year, everybody who's trying to operate in that budget is running at 95%".

Where are the budget negotiations at?

Talks between the government and the executive parties have been taking place for several months now , but earlier this week O'Dowd warned that a "crunch point" is approaching.

On Tuesday, the executive met again, with O'Dowd saying afterwards that he planned to present a series of options to his ministerial colleagues in the days ahead about a way forward.

He did not divulge what those may be, but the government has already said no to a request from the executive to allow a larger chunk of the money in the three-year offer to be spent this year, referred to as "front-loading".

What happens in the absence of a budget?

Without an agreed budget, departments face operating on emergency spending restricted to 95% of the prior year, with warnings that funds could run out by January.

The secretary of state has also warned that a cost-of-living £100 payment cannot be made to households in Northern Ireland until an executive budget is agreed .

That came after the government announced its first budget under Andy Burnham last week, with Northern Ireland getting an additional £270m for public services as a result, of which £131m can be used this year.

Sir Chris has said that he is exploring contingency measures to allow him to pass a budget bill at Westminster, in the event that a deal cannot be reached to do so at Stormont.

stories.body:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”

It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.

MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.

The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025 , a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.

Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.

However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.

after newsletter promotion

The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.

The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.

“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.

As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.

“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.

A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

stories.title: More Mandelson papers set to be published before Christmas
stories.summary: Documents were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a police investigation.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 November 2026

The government is preparing to publish more documents about the appointment of Lord Mandelson as US ambassador.

Batches of papers were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a Metropolitan Police investigation.

The Cabinet Office has now said a number of extra documents will be published, likely before Christmas. Some will still be withheld at the request of the Met.

Cat Little, permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office, said that some of the documents could "now be published without prejudicing their investigation".

The Met Police had launched an investigation over allegations that, while he was serving as a government minister, Lord Mandelson had passed on market-sensitive government information to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Writing to the chair of Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee, Little said: "The Cabinet Office is now beginning the process to prepare these documents so that they may be laid before the House in response to the humble address motion as soon as possible."

She said the documents would be reviewed and in some instances may need to be redacted "for the purposes of avoiding prejudice to national security or international relations".

The process is expected to be completed before Parliament rises for the Christmas recess on 17 December.

Lord Mandelson was arrested on 23 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

He has repeatedly let it be known that he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

"Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing," the Met Police said in a statement.

The lifelong Labour politician became the British ambassador to the US in February 2025, but was sacked in September after Downing Street said new information about the extent of his relationship with Epstein had emerged.

After his sacking, the government - then led by Sir Keir Starmer - was heavily criticised for giving Lord Mandelson the job and in February MPs voted to force the government to publish papers relating to his appointment.

Mike Wood, shadow Cabinet Office minister, said: "We still haven't got to the bottom of the Mandelson scandal.

"Labour did their utmost to hold this information back and it was only released because of the Conservatives humble address."

stories.body:
Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy

US midterm elections – live updates

After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?

US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the midterm elections , lifted by hopes that Donald Trump ’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.

The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party won control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The price of oil dropped sharply as traders assessed the impact of the Democrats’ win on the war in Iran. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell below $100 a barrel for the first time since early October.

In a social media post on Wednesday afternoon, Trump took credit for the jump. “Stock Market just hit another Record High,” he wrote. “Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!”

However, the US dollar fell against the currencies of America’s major trading partners, hitting a one-month low on Wednesday while coming under pressure from falling bond yields. Investors moved into US treasuries, viewed as a haven from the political gridlock anticipated during the rest of Trump’s final term in office.

The dollar index, which measures it against a basket of six currencies, slid to its lowest level in a month, with the pound hitting its highest level since mid-September on the back of a fragile dollar, while the euro also made gains.

The dollar also slid against the yen and the Swiss franc, currencies that traders tend to turn to during times of uncertainty.

Meanwhile, the yield, or interest rate, on the benchmark 10-year US treasury bond has fallen 4.7 basis points to 4.918%. On two-year bonds it has dropped 3.7bps to 4.597%. Yields fall when bond prices rise.

Across the US, voters rejected Trump and the Republican agenda, with the Democrats securing Senate seats in traditional Republican strongholds such as Texas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina.

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the trading platform IG, said: “The scale of the losses will inevitably raise questions about Trump’s ability to push through his agenda over the next two years, and markets are already reacting. The dollar is under pressure as investors reassess the political outlook, while gold and silver are benefiting as safe haven plays.”

Futures trading initially indicated US stock markets would open sharply lower, with the Nasdaq expected to slide on fears over the prospects for AI companies. However, indicators later suggested Wall Street could open higher as Trump’s conciliatory tone and rises on European markets cheered investors.

European markets rose yesterday. London’s FTSE 100 was up 1.8%, Germany’s Dax rose by 2.2%, France’s Cac 40 was 2% higher and Italy’s FTSE MiB index rose by 2.2%.

Bank and clean energy stocks, which have borne the brunt of Trump’s policies, were among the top risers in Europe. Bank stocks rose by 2.8%, while Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems jumped nearly 5% and Ørsted soared 7.4%.

“Some individual names are nursing significant losses today,” said Kathleen Brooks, the UK research director at XTB. “SpaceX is down 5% in the premarket, and Tesla is lower by more than 4%. Elon Musk is considered an anathema to most Democrats.”

Musk, the world’s richest person, pumped $446m (£331m) into the midterms, funding Republican-aligned political action committees and groups.

after newsletter promotion

Brooks said investors were reacting to expectations that a Democrat-controlled Congress could mean greater scrutiny for AI companies, which could also cast doubt on a potential merger of Musk’s two companies.

The price of gold, a traditional haven asset, rose by 2.2%, soaring past $4,000 an ounce.

AI-related shares tumbled during Asian trading hours, on expectations that Democrats will want to bring in greater regulation of the sector.

Chris Turner, the global head of markets at ING, said: “Investors will be parsing what this all means. For example, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race on a ticket of wanting an immediate moratorium on datacentre buildouts.”

He added: “Given AI’s role in powering the US economy , speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capital expenditure plans briefly hit markets.”

Jesper Koll, an expert director at the financial services company Monex Group, said: “The AI momentum has turned negative, with or without the Republicans having a majority. The starting point for financial markets into this election, particularly for the equity market, has been adverse on AI.”

Trump’s style of governing through executive orders has prompted some analysts to question whether the Democrats regaining control of Congress will have much change on US policymaking.

“There’s still a number of areas where Donald Trump can influence the markets – trade and tariffs, foreign policy and existing regulations,” said Tai Hui, a market strategist at JP Morgan Asset Management.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page

Nigel Farage has long been a friend of Donald Trump

Published 5 November 2026

Nigel Farage has said he fears Donald Trump will "aggressively" continue his war with Iran after his "disaster" in the US midterm elections.

The Reform UK leader said the US president was still a friend, but accused him of having "broke a promise" to the American electorate by launching the war.

The war in Iran, which the US began in February 2026, weighed heavily in the midterm election results earlier this week in which the Democrats swept Trump's Republicans out of power in Congress.

Farage, who had initially urged people to support the war, said that following the election results he worried Trump would respond with more strikes on Iran.

Asked how he thinks President Trump will respond, Farage told broadcasters on Thursday: "I suppose I worry that the president will continue aggressively attacking Iran.

"That worries me because that would have even more serious implications for the price of oil, for inflation, for the whole western world".

He acknowledged he had initially supported the war but stressed he "never supported endless war".

Asked if the war was a mistake, he said: "There's no question about it."

The US president had "always kept his promises," added Farage, but "in this case, he said no more foreign wars and here we are in month eight of a war with no sign of ending."

"That and the resulting fuel prices are what in the end has done the damage."

Trump said on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in oil prices.

But he insisted he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran.

This video can not be played

With Congress flipped, what does Trump do next?

In recent weeks, Trump has warned the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.

There have been various warnings , including from politicians in the UK, that Trump may now step up his attacks on Iran but Farage's criticism was more vocal than many have been.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier this week he hoped the midterm results meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".

Farage said he had not spoken to Trump since the midterms but described it as a "complete wipeout" and "an absolute shellacking" for the Republicans.

Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad Published 1 day ago

'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat Published 1 day ago

"Trump has had an amazing career - he has beaten the pollsters, he has gone way beyond expectations," he added.

"This was his last big election and they all say, that all political careers end in failure."

His comments came at an event to announce Reform's first defence spokesperson, after the party was criticised for not having one.

Angus MacIntyre said he had stood down from a 40-year military career, including as a Wing Commander in the Royal Air Force (RAF), to take on the role.

MacIntyre pledged in a speech to end prosecutions of serving military personnel and veterans within the first 100 days of a Reform government.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch had criticised Reform for lacking a defence spokesperson despite having dedicated posts for immigration, the economy and education.

Farage said MacIntyre would form part of "a team we will build to represent us" on the issues of defence, security and cybersecurity.

stories.title: Swinney criticises UK move to ban new North Sea drilling
stories.summary: The first minister has told Holyrood fossil fuels will be required "for some years to come".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 November 2026

First Minister John Swinney says he does not support the UK government's plans to ban any new exploration for oil and gas in the North Sea.

The SNP leader told MSPs fossil fuels would be required "for some years to come".

He argued there was a "rational" case for further exploration if the project's carbon emissions was lower than using imported fuel.

The Scottish government, in its 2023 energy strategy , set out a presumption against new oil and gas drilling.

If passed by MPs, the UK government's Energy Independence Bill would remove the North Sea Transition Authority's ability to grant fresh oil and gas licences, in line with a Labour manifesto pledge not to grant permission for new fields.

It does not affect the decision on whether to allow drilling at Rosebank off Shetland - the UK's largest known untapped field - which was approved in 2022 before being subject to legal challenges.

Swinney has repeatedly refused to be drawn on whether he explicitly supports drilling at Rosebank.

UK government to outlaw new North Sea drilling Published 1 day ago

Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm Published 25 October

Asked about the bill at First Minister's Questions, Swinney said: "The government has set out our view that because we are going to be using oil and gas for years to come there is a rational basis for considering oil and gas developments within our own jurisdiction if they offer lower carbon emissions than imported oil and gas."

He told parliament the UK government's bill includes several measures his government supports, adding: "But we do not support the provisions of that bill in relation to the position on the granting of new licences."

Swinney said this was because "any particular applications need to be considered in relation to their impact on our carbon reduction target and given the fact we are going to be using oil and gas for some years to come".

'Shocking U-turn'

Decisions on new oil and gas licences are made by the UK government.

However, under Nicola Sturgeon's leadership, the Scottish government proposed a presumption against new oil and gas developments.

The Swinney administration appears to have shifted away from that position, especially since the outbreak of war in the Middle East.

Scottish ministers nevertheless continue to stress any oil and gas developments should be compatible with the government's ambitions to cut carbon emissions over time.

Scottish Greens co-leader Gillian Mackay described Swinney's comments as a "shocking U-turn".

She said: "It is a huge departure from only a few years ago when the Scottish government was committed to a presumption against oil and gas.

"When even the UK government is taking a stronger position, it shows how far the SNP has drifted. It is a shameful retreat and a slap in the face for future generations."

Reform UK Scotland leader Malcolm Offord said: "I welcome this breaking news from the first minister as it overrules the SNP's long-standing presumption against new oil and gas exploration."

Rosebank is the UK's largest untapped oil field

Although the UK bill would prevent the granting of new licences, it would allow existing oil and gas fields to provide additional production from within its existing boundaries, or in nearby areas.

The UK government said the move could produce about 60 million barrels of oil and support hundreds of jobs.

It vowed to sustain "growth and investment across North Sea communities as the energy sector transitions".

The wide-ranging bill would also formally scrap gas standing charges and introduce reforms designed to speed up grid connections.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the bill would help to "build a clean energy future which people feel in their pockets, households and communities, ensuring support reaches those who need it most".

The SNP will seek to remove the ban on new oil and gas drilling from the bill. If this does not happen they will oppose the legislation despite supporting other measures contained within it.

stories.title: Drunk and dangerous e-bike riders face on-the-spot fines under crackdown
stories.summary: A consultation will consider fines and other ways to clamp down on dangerous e-bike riders.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 November 2026

People riding drunk or dangerously on e-bikes – and those who jump red lights - could face on-the-spot fines under plans to curb anti-social behaviour.

Firms which run shared e-bike schemes will also be expected to manage their fleets better and provide designated parking areas to keep pavements safe.

They could also be required to take out insurance so people can claim compensation if they are hit by someone on a shared bike.

It's part of a crackdown on what ministers called the "wild west" of e-biking – with a patchwork of rules across the country often leaving the streets unsafe for pedestrians.

A consultation launched on Thursday sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams.

The first e-bikes were launched in Exeter in 2016 and arrived in London a year later, growing to become a popular commuter option.

According to the Greater London Authority, 37 million trips were taken on dockless e-bikes last year – a third more than the previous year.

Shared e-bikes - such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt - make short journeys quick and convenient.

While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes can only be left in specific areas, others have looser rules.

Under the government's proposals, local leaders will be able to license schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks.

Measures could include requiring operators to have a parking plan and to manage fleet sizes and operating areas, so bikes aren't overcrowding streets.

The consultation will also consider ways to tackle antisocial and illegal behaviour, to prevent users from riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements. There will also be clear consequences set out – such as fines - for this type of behaviour.

The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning.

The consultation will last for eight weeks after which the government will draw up legislation to implement the changes.

'Dumped e-scooters force blind people into road' Published 1 April

Red light jumping cyclists offered film over fine Published 14 October

'Our lives will never be the same again after Lime bike crash' Published 29 June

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the e-bike clampdown was a "small but important everyday fix" which would make streets safer.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the government wanted e-bike schemes to "grow in popularity" but acknowledged they were "causing a little bit of nuisance at the moment".

Asked how punishments for dangerous cycling could be enforced, Alexander said licensing rules could allow for fines but added: "What you can't do is legislate for every eventuality, you can't legislate for idiots."

"The police enforce the rules of the road to stop cyclists when they are behaving recklessly but police have got a lot on their plate so individuals have to take some responsibility," she added.

Bosses at Lime, Voi and Bolt all welcomed the proposals, adding that consistent standards being applied across the country would provide clarity and certainty for operators, riders and the general public.

Mike Wordingham from the Royal National Institute for the Blind said 92% of blind and partially sighted people had been forced to walk into roads due to e-bikes blocking pavements.

He welcomed the government's announced but warned that tackling rider behaviour would be "difficult" and said a locally-led approach shouldn't lead to "a patchwork of regulations and inconsistency in implementing them".

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Putin, seen here during a speech in Moscow on Wednesday, has been missing from G20 summits since the Ukraine war

Published 5 November 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Vladimir Putin is not invited to the G20 summit in Manchester.

Asked whether the Russian president would be invited to the annual meeting, which the UK is hosting in November 2027, Burnham said "no" because of sanctions against the Kremlin.

The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

But US president Donald Trump has sparked controversy by inviting Putin to this year's G20, which he will host in Miami in December. The Kremlin has not yet said whether Putin will attend.

Russia is a member of the G20 - a group of 19 nations, the European Union and African Union - while Ukraine is not, but the ongoing war in Ukraine has loomed large over recent summits.

Putin has not attended any major global summit since he launched his invasion and ongoing war in Ukraine.

Asked about inviting him to the G20 in Manchester in 2027, Burnham told The Economist he "will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction" on senior Russian figures.

He said the meeting would provide "a real opportunity" to work with Chinese president Xi Jinping on safety regulations for artificial intelligence (AI).

Pressed on whether the UK could bring the US and China around the same table to agree on global AI supervision, Burnham said: "As I sit here today, that feels challenging, but we've got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI.

"If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.

"So you've got to go into it with that aim."

His decision not to include Putin in next year's gathering in Manchester comes after European diplomats refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in October.

The so-called "family photo" would usually include representatives from all nations in attendance, but this year it was cancelled.

The US decision to invite Lavrov in the first place - which itself came after further public rows between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - also attracted criticism.

Discussing Ukraine, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told Lavrov at the summit: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is."

The UK last hosted the G20 summit in 2009. Next year's two-day event will take place in the Manchester Central Convention Centre in Manchester city centre and host thousands of diplomats and delegates, as well as world leaders.

The government has said it will use its G20 presidency in 2027 to "reinforce global economic stability" and "benefit people in every part of the UK".

stories.title: Could this be the last Bonfire Night for noisy fireworks?
stories.summary: About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, but some campaigners want quieter displays.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 November 2026

Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.

The government is currently considering reducing the noise limit for fireworks by 50% for those bought in shops for private use, after pressure from campaigners concerned about the impact on nervous animals and people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).

Professionally organised displays would continue to have no maximum limit provided the noise level is not harmful to human health.

About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, according to industry figures.

Andy Hubble, of the British Fireworks Association (BFA), said displays had already been getting quieter and a balance must be struck to prevent a black market in noisy fireworks springing up.

The end of October sees the start of several celebrations traditionally marked by fireworks and bonfires, including Halloween on 31 October, Guy Fawkes Night on 5 November, and Diwali, which is on 8 November this year.

The government has said an outright ban on the public buying fireworks would not be proportionate.

But Business Minister Kate Dearden said her department was considering "reforms to fireworks legislation, focused on their key harms associated with their misuse - their noise, and contribution to antisocial behaviour – whilst still allowing individuals to enjoy fireworks safely and responsibly for the important community and cultural celebrations they play a part of."

It is already illegal to sell fireworks to under 18s, or to set fireworks off after 23:00, with exemptions for special occasions including Bonfire Night, Diwali, New Year's Eve and Chinese New Year.

But campaigners have raised concerns about the impact of loud bangs on nervous pets.

Dog owner Katherine Alderson, from Clacton-on-Sea, told BBC Breakfast: "It's a nightmare every single year.

"This year I've actually barricaded my bedroom window with numerous layers of insulation to try and keep out the noise of fireworks."

Asked whether reducing the bangs would take the fun out of fireworks, she said she believed displays "should be about the lights and colours" and suggested "a complete ban" on the sale of fireworks to the general public could be the solution.

A woman enjoys fireworks in a crowd of people

But other campaigners say a ban is not needed, including Alan Friggieri, from the charity Combat Stress, which supports veterans with PTSD.

Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons' Business Committee, Friggieri said calls to their helpline jump at this time of year because loud bangs can trigger PTSD symptoms.

"Nothing quite sounds like an AK47 other than fireworks going off - it's that crackle," one veteran who had been shot multiple times had told him.

Friggieri said veterans need to be able to plan around key dates, but he said he was not calling for a ban, because his organisation understands the cultural importance of firework displays.

Calling for better enforcement of existing rules by police to stop antisocial behaviour, BFA vice chairman Hubble warned a ban in Ireland had seen a flourishing black market in firework sales.

"There is a real risk here that if we make fireworks quieter that there is still a demand then we could create an illegal market where fireworks are coming in through internet sales and white van sales," he told BBC Breakfast.

"At the moment we have a really well-regulated market where we have enforcers that know the products and can test them but as soon as these products go undercover then we lose that.

"We could actually create a louder and noisier environment because those are the sorts of fireworks that we're seeing coming in through illegal sales on the internet."

Asked whether it was true that displays were getting noisier, Hubble said: "No, no, it's a lot quieter than it used to be - we used to have bangers and air bombs and and screamer rockets that used to be on sale and they were withdrawn from sale."

The government is considering reducing the maximum noise limit from the current 120dB, equivalent toa thunderclap, to 110dB, which is equivalent to a car horn.

Hubble said a BFA assessment of firework sales shows a 50% noise reduction to 110 dB would impact up to 60% of firework sales to the general public.

Lowering levels to 90DB, equivalent to a lawnmower, as some campaigners want, would affect about 95% of fireworks.

"That's effectively a ban on consumer fireworks, not a modest reduction in noise," he said.

RSPCA advice for people with nervous pets:

Stay calm and show your pet that all is well

Put on music or the TV to help mask firework sounds

Close any windows and do what you can to block out both the noise and the flashes

Keep your environment secure: make sure your pet can't escape if there's a sudden noise

stories.body:
John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff

W ith four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic.

The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points.

They had been punished as part of a “special campaign to crack down on match-fixing, gambling and corruption in the football industry”, said a joint statement from the Chinese Football Association, the Ministry of Public Security and the General Administration of Sport at the time.

Chengdu were one of the seven to start on zero, above the defending champions Shanghai Port, who lost five points, and the runners-up Shanghai Shenhua who were hit with 10. It robbed the usual favourites of energy and it was all a bit surreal.

It almost felt over as soon as it started with Chengdu opening up a big lead, dropping just two points from the first 12 games while the usual powers struggled to get going.

Chengdu is a major city known more for its fiery Sichuan cuisine, genteel temples and cute pandas than football, despite English attempts to change that. In 2006, Sheffield United bought a local club but the Chengdu Blades were eventually dissolved in 2015. Four years later, City Football Group bought a stake in Sichuan Jiuniu but then moved the club to the southern city of Shenzhen in 2024.

Chengdu Rongcheng were formed in 2018, coming up through the divisions to finally, this season, be within touching distance of the championship. But just two wins from the past 13 and three defeats in a row mean the leaders are not limping to the line but have collapsed right next to it.

It should have been over weeks ago. On 10 October, more than 40,000 fans were ready to celebrate the title but an added‑time goal from Alberto Quiles gave Tianjin Jinmen Tiger a 1-0 win and postponed the celebrations. Next up was a trip to Shanghai Port but that ended in a 3-0 defeat. The penultimate game of the season came against challengers Dalian Yingbo, when again, just avoiding defeat was needed. It was another painful experience as they lost 1-0 after missing a first-half penalty and having a 90th-minute equaliser ruled out by the video assistant referee.

Chengdu have not scored in almost seven hours of football while Dalian are the form team with four consecutive wins. If they win a fifth against Tianjin then Chengdu need a point at fourth‑placed Shandong Taishan as the league is decided by head-to-head results before goal difference. Not many think they will. Even fewer hope so. Dalian and the 60,000 fans who attend home games are the people’s choice. Chengdu are not popular because their fans have developed a poor reputation. Last November, the club were fined about $70,000 (£52,200) after some home supporters racially abused Henan FC’s Ghanaian striker Frank Acheampong, just weeks after a punishment of $3,000 after travelling supporters at a Champions League game in South Korea threw bottles at the Ulsan HD players.

Whatever happens it is an unexpected and dramatic ending to a season that started in shock and the usual negative international headlines that surround Chinese football. The grandstand finish is welcome and average attendances have risen. They are poised to finish at about 30,000, a considerable jump from 25,755 last season and, by some distance, the best in Asia. Regional leagues have been enjoying some popularity too, showing that there is genuine love for the game in the country; a passion that grows better when it is organic from the bottom rather than organised from the top.

after newsletter promotion

The national side is still a problem, though, and even for a fanbase well accustomed to disappointment the recent 5-0 defeat against Palestine at home, the fourth-biggest loss in history, was tough to take. As one journalist said, being thrashed by Brazil, Japan and Wales is one thing, but Palestine was another. There were some mitigating circumstances in that a number of national team players were at the Asian Games, where China actually performed well, losing narrowly against South Korea in the bronze final.

There are signs that the gap behind Korea is not as wide as it used to be. China reached the final of the under-17 and under-23 Asian championships this year before losing both against Japan. Compared with the rest of Asia’s best, young Chinese players are closing the gap at a technical and tactical level. Exporting more players to Europe is necessary to play at a higher level and if that happens, that senior national shirt may feel a little lighter.

Failure can, however, be hard to shake off as Chengdu Rongcheng may well find out if they mess this up.

stories.title: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
stories.summary: Co-founder of Palestine Action, Huda Ammori, is challenging the government's decision to proscribe the group.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Supporters of Palestine Action were arrested outside the Supreme Court, where a hearing over the group's ban began on Wednesday

Published 4 November 2026

The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience from law-abiding protesters, the Supreme Court has been told.

Opening a major legal challenge to the group's proscription last year, lawyers for co-founder Huda Ammori said that no other protest organisation had been treated the same way.

They told the five justices that the UK's highest court had never before had to consider whether banning a group under terrorism legislation was compatible with freedom of speech and protest.

Twenty-seven protesters were arrested outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday as the hearing took place, the Metropolitan Police said.

Lawyers for Ammori told the court that thousands of elderly people, many veterans of other radical causes, had been arrested for holding up signs supportive of the group since its proscription.

Home Office figures seen by the BBC indicate that there have been more than 4,000 arrests so far at protests in which people have held up signs supportive of the group.

In practice, many demonstrators have been arrested more than once, with 1,200 charges authorised by prosecutors to date. Those trials are in limbo until the outcome of this case.

Henry Blaxland KC told the court that "far from depriving Palestine Action of the oxygen of publicity" and "far from discrediting its brand", proscription of the group has had the opposite effect.

"All it's done is to pour fuel on to a fire of one of the most publicly-contested issues of our time," he said.

"It was disproportionate to do that and in my submission completely unnecessary."

During often tense exchanges with the judges, Ammori's team accepted that Palestine Action could not be described as an ordinary and peaceful protest group.

They said that its members had carried out "direct action" protests by occupying or vandalising firms linked to Israel's military - with only three of 385 incidents assessed by the Home Secretary as constituting an offence under the Terrorism Act.

The UK's definition of terrorism includes incidents of serious damage to property for a cause - and at least two break-ins at defence firms have been described in criminal courts as having caused millions in damage.

Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that the judges had to put aside allegations of criminality - for which the state had many powers - and consider whether the Home Secretary's decision to label the group as terrorists had been disproportionate.

"Palestine Action was proscribed on the basis of less than one per cent of its actions over five years assessed as falling within the outer limits of a definition of terrorism," he said.

"The Home Secretary's own experts confirmed the vast majority of its direct action would not constitute an act of terrorism on the basis that any damage to property is typically more minor. Common tactics include graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation, and lock-ons."

One Palestine Action member has been convicted and jailed of fracturing a police officer's back with a sledgehammer - but the court was told that the group had never advocated such violence.

Opposition from Jewish groups

The Supreme Court has received arguments from free speech campaigners, arguing the ban interferes with the right to protest.

But another submission from a coalition of Jewish groups argued that Palestine Action was a "sinister" organisation intent on attacking its community interests.

"The Court of Appeal [following earlier hearings] rightly concluded that PA is a violent organisation concerned in terrorism with a wide range of targets," said Adam Wagner KC in written submissions for the Jewish communal groups.

He continued: "Its activities are often undertaken covertly with no suggestion of restraint or proportionality, and that at the point it was proscribed it had an escalating trajectory of seriousness and an expanding focus."

Wagner said Palestine Action's "crosshairs" had moved from targeting Elbit, a defence firm with an Israeli parent company, to "figures or institutions deemed by PA to be 'Zionist'".

"Because most British Jews and Jewish institutions have a connection with Israel, a campaign against institutions PA's activists consider to be 'complicit' with Israel is, in practice, a campaign that threatens the mainstream Jewish community," he said.

However, Jewish Bloc, a group that campaigns in solidarity with Palestinians, told has also written to the court to say that claims that PA targeted their community were a "fundamental misrepresentation of the underlying evidence".

Rachel Scott KC, for the organisation, told the justices: "Neither the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) nor the Community Security Trust (CST) have any democratic mandate. Claims that either organisation can be viewed as the voice of British Jews must therefore be viewed with very significant caution.

"The framing of PA as an organisation which threatened and intimidated 'the Jewish Community' is demonstrably false and a deliberate elision. The evidence instead shows that it targeted entities, organisations and institutions with an established link to Israel's illegal activities against the Palestinian people."

The case continues on Thursday with a judgment expected at a later date.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Republicans’ crushing setback will play out in stock markets, inflation, interest rates and economic growth

Donald Trump’s loss of control of the House of Representatives and the Senate has put the world economy on notice for an unpredictable final two years of his presidential term.

After Democrats swept aside his Republican party in the midterm elections, analysts said the prospect of a highly erratic lame-duck president would have significant implications for financial markets, growth, inflation, government borrowing costs and living standards.

Here are the biggest expected consequences for the US economy and for other countries.

Stock markets

Markets initially dropped in early trading in Asia overnight but rallied as investors weighed up the midterm results.

Investors typically dislike uncertainty and political chaos. The fact that the president conceded the result and acknowledged the impact of the Iran war has been taken as a positive in markets. However, his warning that he will become “Mr Veto” raises the prospect of a turbulent finale to his time in the White House.

Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg, said the result showed that US voters had “rejected Trump and his somewhat authoritarian penchant for crony capitalism. [That] shows that US institutions and its checks and balances work. That is a positive, in my view.”

Much of the outlook for stock markets, inflation and growth is contingent on the war in the Middle East and the pace of the advance of artificial intelligence.

Traders expect the Democrats to take a tougher line on AI regulation and the datacentre rollout, raising questions over a driver of stock market growth. There are also concerns that Trump, with the midterms out of the way and his control over domestic policy weakened, could take a more aggressive approach to foreign policy, with the potential to intensify the war in Iran.

Inflation

The cost to US households from surging inflation triggered by a deeply unpopular war, alongside a chaotic tariff policy that has devastated small businesses, was key to the midterm result. US diesel prices surged to a record high in August , while the headline inflation rate has risen to 3.7%.

The US-Israeli invasion of Iran, leading to the closure of the critical strait of Hormuz, reignited global inflationary pressures amid the biggest energy price shock of the modern age.

The oil price fell back on Wednesday, dropping by as much as 9% to trade below $100 a barrel for the first time in a month, as investors digested the midterm results amid hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough on Iran. Trading at about $94, Brent crude, the international benchmark, remains significantly higher than its prewar level of about $70. As a consequence, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects global headline inflation to rise to 4.7% this year, with energy-importing countries hardest hit.

The possibility of Trump ramping up hostilities against Iran would add to the inflationary shock, but it would also further add to his unpopularity.

Interest rates

Higher inflation has forced central banks to raise interest rates, with the US Federal Reserve defying pressure from Trump by increasing the cost of borrowing for the first time since 2023.

Against a volatile backdrop in the war and as inflationary pressures persist, investors anticipate at least one more rate increase from the Fed. The Bank of England is expected on Thursday to raise rates , while the European Central Bank is also expected to push up borrowing costs.

After losing control of Congress, the Republicans will lack the votes to confirm new appointments to critical public bodies, including new Fed governors. Trump could still use his veto powers, which can be overturned only if two-thirds of both chambers agree.

Government finances

Higher inflation and interest rates triggered by the Iran war have driven up borrowing costs, adding to the pressure on countries with high levels of public debt.

In the US, the logjammed political system will face its first major test on 11 December, when politicians have to agree to authorise government spending to avoid a shutdown . The gridlock could prevent Trump from launching new tax and spending measures, which could cut two ways, restricting the capacity for fiscal stimulus to boost the economy, but also limiting a further rise in borrowing and debt.

Analysts say the crushing midterm defeats for Maga candidates will hurt the president’s authority and could pave the way for more cooperation between Republicans and Democrats in Congress.

Economic growth

Analysts say political turbulence and presidential actions on trade and immigration could put US growth at risk, but inflation and, most importantly, the prospects for de-escalation in the Middle East are the main factors to watch.

Investors are wary that a clampdown by the Democrats on AI could hit investment and growth in the US. The spillovers from the tech boom have been felt around the globe, with AI investment helping to bolster the UK economy.

However, tech industry leaders were already cooling on the rollout of AI amid concerns over cyber risks. Many investors also feared the emergence of a bubble in the US stock market. Analysts at Allianz say the scale of AI investment, and its capacity to power global economic growth, could mean the left-right political playbook is less predictable than in the past. Environmental and social impacts are also increasingly important considerations.

As recently as last month the IMF forecast that US growth would remain stable at 2.3% this year and next, despite the heightened risks to activity caused by the Iran war and the uncertain path for AI investment.

Analysts at Berenberg said US growth could slow to about 1.5% in 2028 amid political gridlock, a slowdown over AI and a drag from Trump’s crackdown on immigration. As a result, the US would contribute less to global growth than before, they said.

stories.body:
Purchasing manager’s index at eight-month high, bolstered by spending on AI as firms regain momentum lost to Iran war

The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday after a closely watched survey showed growth across the UK’s services sector leapt last month to an eight-month high, bolstered by spending on artificial intelligence.

S&P Global’s survey of the services sector in October showed businesses regained much of the momentum they lost after the start of the Iran war, but also felt the impact of a renewed spurt of input price inflation, which accelerated to a five-month high.

Officials at the Bank have become concerned about inflation after the consumer prices index (CPI) rose from 3.1% in August to 3.5% in September .

While the nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC), which sets interest rates, has been split in recent months , a majority is expected to vote on Thursday for 0.25 percentage point increase to 4%.

Tim Moore, the economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a survey of the manufacturing sector earlier this week also showed businesses facing strong price pressures.

He said: “These signals underscore the near-certainty of a Bank of England rate hike in November and collectively raise the likelihood of further Bank of England policy tightening into 2027.”

Financial markets expect three further increases in the cost of borrowing, although most City economists believe inflation is likely to peak in the spring of next year, allowing the Bank to limit the number of extra interest rate rises to one or two.

Moore said service providers indicated the fastest upturn in activity since February and “a solid rebound in new orders”.

The S&P Global services purchasing manager’s index (PMI), which gauges growth across sector, rose from 52.1 to 52.8. A reading above 50 indicates a period of expansion.

Bigger workloads prompted businesses in the services industry to take on additional staff in October, the survey found.

This ended two years of continuous job cutting across the sector, with many businesses during that period saying that they were responding to higher labour and business costs, or not replacing employees who left.

Moore said the survey suggested an “increase in economic resilience despite challenges from geopolitical tensions, elevated cost pressures and subdued consumer confidence”.

“Greater workloads were attributed to an improved pipeline of sales opportunities, particularly those linked to AI investment spending,” he added.

The sector has benefited from the demand for AI applications and software services associated with the boom in datacentre construction.

Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the economic forecasters the Item Club, said official data also pointed to a surge in activity in the IT and professional services sectors.

after newsletter promotion

He cautioned that growth in business-to-business services was not being matched on the high street, which has continued to be badly affected by a dip in consumer confidence.

“With at least some of that strength reflecting businesses’ rapid adoption of AI technologies, we expect pockets of strength to sustain momentum into next year. But in a two-speed economy, consumer-facing services will come under increasing pressure as households’ spending power is squeezed,” Swannell said.

He added: “An interest rate hike looks nailed on at tomorrow’s MPC meeting. And today’s data only adds to the weight of evidence.”

Moore said about four in 10 of the services sector survey panel reported an increase in their input prices, while only 1% experienced a decline.

It is unclear how much services firms will pass on higher input costs to consumers, pushing up inflation. Some members of the MPC have said they are prepared to wait for more evidence while others have indicated they will vote to quell even modest increases in prices.

Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said there was a sign that services businesses were absorbing costs, but not by enough to prevent a rate rise.

The services output price balance dropped to 56.9, from 57.8 in September. “We estimate this is consistent with underlying services inflation rising about 4.1%, down from the latest official reading of 4.4% but still too high for the MPC to stand pat,” Wood said.

Meanwhile, inflation in the eurozone rose to a three-year high of 4% last month on surging energy and food costs, up from 3.8% in September. The increase makes a rate rise in December by the European Central Bank more likely after it left borrowing costs unchanged last week.
